title: Attribution
summary: Attribution is the analytic judgement that links a set of observed activity to a responsible actor, and it is one of the most overclaimed products in cyber threat intelligence. Analysts distinguish at least three questions that are routinely conflated: technical attribution of tooling and infrastructure to a cluster of activity, operational attribution of that cluster to a consistent set of people and their tradecraft, and strategic or political attribution of those people to a state, sponsor or criminal organisation. Each step is weaker than the last and requires evidence of a different kind, so confidence should fall as the claim becomes more consequential. The core technical difficulty is that tooling, malware families, infrastructure and even credentials are shared, resold, stolen or deliberately planted. False flags are cheap: strings, language artefacts, time zone artefacts and reused code can all be inserted to mislead. Mature practice therefore relies on corroboration across independent sources, on clustering by infrastructure and capability rather than by a single indicator, and on structured analytic techniques that force the analyst to argue the alternative hypothesis. Naming conventions matter as well. Tracking a cluster with a neutral designator keeps the technical analysis separable from the attribution claim, whereas reusing a named actor label imports assumptions about intent and sponsorship that the evidence may not support. Public attribution also carries legal, diplomatic and operational consequences, so it is normally a leadership decision informed by intelligence rather than a side effect of a technical report. Defensively, attribution rarely changes the immediate response, because containment, eradication and recovery depend on what the adversary can do, not on who they are, though it does shape long-term risk, control investment and intelligence sharing.
objectives: You will be able to separate technical, operational and strategic attribution and state the evidence each requires.
You will be able to argue an alternative hypothesis and identify the false flag opportunities in a given evidence set.
You will be able to cluster activity by infrastructure and capability instead of relying on a single indicator.
You will be able to write an attribution judgement with explicit confidence and a clear statement of assumptions.
You will be able to explain why neutral cluster designators reduce analytic bias compared with named actor labels.
You will be able to describe how attribution affects long-term risk decisions while leaving incident response largely unchanged.

beginner.definition: Attribution is the work of deciding who is behind a cyber attack. You study the clues and try to name the person, group or country responsible. It is a judgement, not a fact, so you should always say how sure you are.
beginner.whyItMatters: Knowing who attacked you rarely changes how you clean up. You still remove the malware and reset the passwords. Attribution matters for the long game. It shapes which risks you track, where you spend money and who you warn. Bad attribution is dangerous. If you blame the wrong group, you may miss the real threat and make a serious political mistake.
howItWorks: Collect the evidence. Gather file names, network addresses, timestamps and the tools the attacker used.
Group the activity into a cluster. Give it a neutral name like Cluster A, so you do not bias yourself.
Separate three questions. Which tools, which people, and which sponsor or state? Each answer needs stronger proof.
Look for false flags. Attackers plant other languages and time zones to make you blame someone else.
Check independent sources. One report is weak, but several sources that agree raise your confidence.
State your judgement with a confidence level, and list the evidence that would prove you wrong.
beginner.example: Imagine a threatening note is pushed under your door. The handwriting looks foreign, but anyone can copy a style. It might be a neighbour, or someone far away trying to frame that neighbour. You would not accuse anyone based on one clue. You would look for fingerprints, camera footage and a motive. Cyber attribution works the same way. One clue is never enough, and clever attackers leave misleading clues on purpose.
takeaways: Attribution is a careful judgement with a confidence level, never a certain fact.
Attackers plant false clues, so cross-check several independent sources before you blame anyone.
Who attacked you rarely changes your cleanup, but it shapes long-term risk decisions.

exercises.title: Attribution - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Attribution - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Attribution - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Attribution - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
